claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittle behavior.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries cause high local stress concentrations and premature microcracking in the untreated alloy.
Adding approximately 0.1–0.5 wt% boron during melting or casting is the proposed intervention.
Boron added during processing will segregate to lamellar colony boundaries.
Boron segregation will transform dual-phase lamellar interfaces into disordered complexions.
Boron segregation reduces local interfacial energy.
The resulting disordered complexions are more receptive barriers for dislocations than the original sharp interfaces.
Boron-induced complexions facilitate more uniform dislocation transmission across interfaces.
Improved dislocation transmission reduces concentrated dislocation pile-ups at internal interfaces.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups lowers interface-associated local stress concentrations.
Lower local stress concentrations delay microcrack nucleation during tensile straining.
The boron-modified alloy will have significantly greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the untreated alloy.
The boron-modified alloy will maintain or slightly increase tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The proposed effect is expected under standard room-temperature tensile-test conditions.
The effect may vary with strain rate or testing temperature.
